newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac wins agreement for Congo truce - aide.
newsitem.headline: Chirac wins agreement for Congo truce - aide.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac has won agreement for a ceasefire from the warring sides in Congo, his office said on Monday.
Chirac's spokeswoman said he had received verbal agreement for a ceasefire in telephone conversations with President Pascal Lissouba and his opponent, former president Denis Sassou-Nguesso.

Chirac asked the two adversaries "to decide on a ceasefire as soon as possible and accept the mediation of (Gabon President) Omar Bongo to seek a political solution and he obtained their agreement in principle," spokeswoman Catherine Colonna told reporters.
She said Chirac told the two men resorting to arms was unacceptable and "there can be no military solution to a political problem". Chirac earlier spoke to Bongo, she said.
Chirac's intervention came as France, the former colonial power, sent more troops to embattled Brazzaville, bringing the number of its troops there to 1,200.
Their main mission was to help evacuate hundreds of French and other foreigners to escape the fighting between political and ethnic militias.
Amid reports of hostility towards French nationals, 460 French residents were flown to Libreville, in neighbouring Gabon, and 100 more were to be evacuated later in the day.

Paris announced it was sending more troops after a French soldier was killed and five were wounded in a clash with local irregulars while rescuing foreigners. It boosted the number of reinforcements after heavy fighting resumed between forces loyal to President Pascal Lissouba and ex-president Denis Sassou Nguesso's militia.

France's junior cooperation minister Charles Josselin said on television his new left-wing government aimed to change the way France operated in Africa, ending a tradition of influence through semi-clandestine Gaullist networks.
Josselin, a Socialist whose brief is relations with former French possessions in the Third World, said the French troops in Congo-Brazzaville would remain impartial "for the time being".
He said government and rebels were both to blame for the breakdown of order, and blamed the "Gaullist networks" for France's slipping position in Africa.

"They already have a very large part of responsibility for France being on the wrong side in Zaire... and the death of Jacques Foccart (veteran Gaullist string-puller in Africa who died in March) is an opportunity we must seize to change this situation," Josselin told LCI television.
Sassou Nguesso, speaking to LCI from Brazzaville, placed the blame for fighting on pro-government militias which he said were trained by Israeli mercenaries.
He denied any anti-French feelings among his partisans and said French casualties resulted from government fire.
He said he still hoped elections, scheduled for July, would take place and welcomed foreign mediation offers.
Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin took office only last week, and the fighting provided a first test of his government and "cohabitation" with conservative President Jacques Chirac.
Analysts said Chirac and Jospin would be keen to present a united front in a crisis endangering French lives, but differences on African policy were likely to emerge later.
Some African experts have evoked a "domino theory", forecasting that the upheaval in Zaire would spill over into its neighbours and destabilise other former French colonies.
